title: Gravitational Force and Central Field Mechanics
short_intro: Gravitational force is a fundamental universal attractive interaction acting between any two point masses. It is a conservative central force governed by Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Newton's law of gravitation, variation of acceleration due to gravity (g) with depth and altitude, gravitational potential energy, escape velocity, and Kepler's laws of planetary motion.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Gravitational field and potential for continuous mass distributions (spherical shell, solid sphere), planetary motion under inverse-square central forces, Kepler's equation, and non-inertial frame transformations involving centrifugal and Coriolis forces.

prerequisites: Vector calculus and spherical polar coordinate systems
Newton's laws of motion and kinematics
Conservation laws of linear and angular momentum

concept_notes.heading: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
bullets: States that every particle attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
Expressed mathematically as F = G (m<sub>1</sub>m<sub>2</sub> / r<sup>2</sup>) r̂, where G is the universal gravitational constant.
It acts along the line joining the point masses, making it a central force and hence a conservative force field.

concept_notes.heading: Gravitational Field and Potential
bullets: Gravitational field intensity E is defined as the gravitational force experienced by a unit test mass placed at that point: E = F / m.
Gravitational potential V at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to that point without acceleration.
The relation between field and potential is given by the negative gradient: E = -∇V.

concept_notes.heading: Variation of Acceleration Due to Gravity (g)
bullets: At altitude h above the Earth's surface (for h << R), g' = g(1 - 2h/R).
At depth d below the Earth's surface, g' = g(1 - d/R), assuming a uniform density Earth model.
Due to the Earth's diurnal rotation with angular velocity omega, the effective gravity at latitude lambda is given by g' = g - Rω<sup>2</sup> cos<sup>2</sup>λ.

concept_notes.heading: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
bullets: First Law (Law of Orbits): Planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun located at one of the two foci.
Second Law (Law of Areas): The position vector of a planet from the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time, which is a direct consequence of conservation of angular momentum.
Third Law (Law of Periods): The square of the orbital period of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit (T<sup>2</sup> ∝ a<sup>3</sup>).

derivations.title: Variation of Gravitational Acceleration with Depth
derivations.conditions: Assuming the Earth is a homogeneous sphere of radius R and uniform density ρ.
steps: Consider a point at depth d below the surface. The effective distance from the center is r = R - d.
According to Newton's shell theorem, the mass outside this radius sphere exerts no net gravitational force on a body inside.
The effective mass causing attraction is M' = (ρ)(4/3)π(R - d)<sup>3</sup> and total mass M = (ρ)(4/3)πR<sup>3</sup>, giving M' = M(R - d / R)<sup>3</sup>.
The gravitational acceleration at depth d is g' = G M' / (R - d)<sup>2</sup> = G M (R - d) / R<sup>3</sup>.
Substituting GM / R<sup>2</sup> = g, we obtain g' = g (1 - d / R).

derivations.title: Orbital Velocity and Total Energy of a Satellite
derivations.conditions: Satellite of mass m revolving in a circular orbit of radius r around a central mass M.
steps: Equate the gravitational force to the required centripetal force: G M m / r<sup>2</sup> = m v<sup>2</sup> / r.
Solve for orbital velocity: v = \sqrt{G M / r}.
Kinetic energy K = (1/2) m v<sup>2</sup> = G M m / (2r).
Potential energy U = - G M m / r.
Total mechanical energy E = K + U = - G M m / (2r).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Variation of g with Distance from Earth's Center
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph with r on the x-axis and g(r) on the y-axis. For r ≤ R, a straight line passing through the origin with positive slope. For r > R, a curve falling sharply as 1/r<sup>2</sup>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Inside the Earth, g increases linearly with radius. At the surface, it achieves its maximum value g. Outside the Earth, it drops inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in TGT/PGT conceptual MCQs regarding turning points and continuity at r = R.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Effective Potential Energy Curve for Central Orbits
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Graph of U_eff(r) vs r featuring a centrifugal barrier term (L<sup>2</sup> / 2mr<sup>2</sup>) and attractive gravitational potential (-GMm/r), showing a minimum representing stable circular orbits.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The minimum of the effective potential corresponds to the stable equilibrium radius where attractive gravitational force equals the centrifugal force.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Evaluated in PGT questions to determine apsidal distances and stability of orbits.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Cavendish Torsion Balance Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup showing two small masses on a light horizontal rod suspended by a fine quartz fiber, attracted by two large lead spheres.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used to measure the weak gravitational force between laboratory masses, enabling the direct experimental determination of the universal gravitational constant G.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested as a factual conceptual question regarding the experimental verification of G.

solved_numericals.question: At what depth below the surface of the Earth does the acceleration due gravity become 75% of its value at the surface? (Assume Earth radius R = 6400 km)
solution_steps: Formula for gravity at depth d is g' = g (1 - d / R).

solved_numericals.question: A satellite is orbiting the Earth in a circular orbit of radius 4R (where R is the Earth's radius). What additional velocity must be imparted to the satellite so that it escapes the Earth's gravitational field?
solution_steps: Calculate the current orbital velocity v_o at r = 4R: v_o = \sqrt{GM / 4R} = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{GM / R}.
Calculate the escape velocity v_e from the orbit radius r = 4R: v_e = \sqrt{2GM / 4R} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{GM / R}.
The required additional velocity (boost Δv) is Δv = v_e - v_o.

solved_numericals.question: Two uniform solid spheres of mass M and radius R are touching each other. Find the gravitational potential energy of this two-body system.
solution_steps: The distance between the centers of the two touching spheres is r = 2R.
The gravitational potential energy of a two-point mass system is U = - \frac{G m_1 m_2}{r}.
Substitute m_1 = M, m_2 = M, and r = 2R into the formula.

assumptions_and_limitations: Newton's law of gravitation assumes instantaneous propagation of gravitational interaction, which is a limitation rectified by General Relativity where gravity propagates at the speed of light.
The uniform density shell theorems assume isotropic and spherically symmetric mass distributions, failing for irregularly shaped celestial bodies unless expanded in multipole moments.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Gravitational potential inside a solid sphere is zero because the field inside is zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: The gravitational field is zero at the center, but the potential is non-zero and finite.
common_misconceptions.why: Potential is the integral of the field from infinity; even if the field vanishes at a point or inside a shell, integrating from the surface inward accumulates potential.

common_misconceptions.wrong: An astronaut inside an orbiting satellite experiences zero gravitational force.
common_misconceptions.correct: The astronaut experiences free fall where gravity provides the centripetal acceleration, resulting in a sensation of apparent weightlessness.
common_misconceptions.why: The gravitational force at orbital heights is about 90% of surface gravity; the normal reaction from the floor is zero because both astronaut and spacecraft accelerate equally towards the Earth.

quick_revision: Gravitational force is a conservative central force yielding an inverse-square field law.
Acceleration due to gravity varies as g' = g(1 - h/R) for small heights and g' = g(1 - d/R) for depths.
Orbital energy is negative, demonstrating bound states, whereas total energy ≥ 0 corresponds to unbound parabolic or hyperbolic escape trajectories.
